meaning: Titles and reading notes drafted by an AI agent in the register of the paper they annotate. No mathematician has reviewed them.

notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Script: Each command must satisfy the grammatical conditions of the version in force where it begins. A version declaration changes that version for later commands, and a command that stops reading may occur only last. The relation does not enforce well-sortedness, solver execution modes or the official benchmark requirement that version metadata occur exactly once as the first command.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsCommand: This relation combines the token sequence of a command with the command's version-dependent grammatical conditions. It therefore includes the grammar's nonempty and equal-length list requirements. It describes a recognised command, not its execution: no assertion stack, model, satisfiability result or solver response is part of the relation.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsSExpr: A token sequence represents a specified S-expression exactly when that expression satisfies the selected version's grammatical condition and writing it yields those tokens. The relation is about tokens already supplied to the grammar, not arbitrary source characters. In particular, recognising legal spellings and decoding quoted literals are responsibilities of the preceding lexical stage.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsSort: A token sequence represents a specified sort when the sort satisfies the selected version's grammatical condition and is written by exactly that sequence. This matches the displayed syntax production at the token level. It does not establish that the sort's symbols are declared or applied with their declared arities; those are separate semantic requirements.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsTerm: A token sequence represents a specified term when that term satisfies the grammatical restrictions for the selected version and writing it yields those tokens. The condition combines the term forms with their required nonempty lists. It does not require a signature or prove well-sortedness, variable scope, substitution laws or logical equivalences between term forms.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.AttributeValue: Attribute values have three represented forms: a special constant, a symbol, or a list of S-expressions. A keyword or reserved word cannot appear as a lone value, though either may occur inside a list when the version permits it. This follows the displayed production; the prose description as S-expressions other than keywords is less restrictive about reserved words.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.Valid: The command must be available in the selected version and satisfy the grammar's nonemptiness, list-length and recursive syntax conditions. Version 2.7 admits arbitrary terms as check-sat-assuming arguments; versions 2.5 and 2.6 admit only propositional literals. These conditions do not require Boolean assumptions, maintain an assertion stack, enforce solver execution modes or determine command responses.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.tokens: The formal definition writes the tokens of each represented command, including names, arguments and parentheses. It also represents the older literal-only form of check-sat-assuming separately from the version 2.7 form with term arguments. The token sequence alone does not establish version availability, the required list lengths, or the operational effects of executing a command.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.DatatypeDec.Val: The datatype declaration must contain at least one constructor, and each constructor's selector sorts must satisfy their grammatical conditions. This does not establish the paper's requirements on distinct names, matching numbers of sort parameters, permitted recursive occurrences or well-foundedness of mutually recursive datatypes. Those restrictions need information beyond the syntax of this declaration.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDec.Val: This condition checks the grammatical form of each parameter sort and the result sort. It does not establish that those sorts exist in the current signature, that parameters have distinct names, or that the function name is fresh. The formal definition is one part of recognising declaration syntax, rather than the full test required before introducing a function.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDef.Val: The parameter sorts, result sort and defining term must satisfy their grammatical conditions. The definition does not check that the term has the declared result sort, that its variables are in scope, or that recursive references are permitted. In particular, the difference between ordinary and recursive function definitions is not settled by this condition alone.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Index.Valid: Numeral indices are admitted in every supported version; symbol indices are admitted from version 2.5 onward. This condition does not check the characters of the numeral or symbol. The choice of 2.5 follows the paper's change log, although Appendix A's historical note gives 2.6. Both alternatives are available for the version 2.7 page.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.Valid: A single symbol or wildcard must be available in the selected version. A constructor pattern must have at least one argument, and every argument must be a permitted symbol or wildcard. The formal condition does not check constructor names, argument sorts, distinct pattern variables or coverage of a datatype's constructors. These are additional requirements in the paper.
The formal condition requires the identifier's indices and any attached sort to satisfy their grammatical conditions in the selected version. It does not determine the symbol's rank or check that the attached sort is one of its possible result sorts. Those are requirements of well-sortedness in the paper, which are not supplied by this grammatical condition.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SExpr.Valid: This condition restricts reserved-word atoms to versions 2.6 and 2.7 and requires the word to belong to that version's reserved set. Lists must satisfy the same condition recursively. Other atoms are admitted without further tests here because their spelling belongs to the lexical stage. The declaration supplies version restrictions, not the whole definition of S-expression syntax.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Sort.Valid: A sort satisfies this condition when its identifier has permitted indices and all its argument sorts satisfy the same grammatical condition. It does not consult a signature, check the declared arity of a sort symbol, or distinguish a sort parameter from a sort constructor. The paper's rules for well-formed sorts require that additional information.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term: The represented application form has a qualified identifier in function position, as in the main term production. Section 3.9 additionally permits omitting @ when applying any term of monomorphic map sort, allowing a term in that position. That broader shorthand is not represented here; it can instead be written with explicit @. The representation also allows empty lists, with required nonemptiness checked separately.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.Valid: The formal definition enforces nonempty lists where the grammar uses one or more repetitions, permits match from version 2.6 and lambda from version 2.7, and applies grammatical conditions recursively. It does not check variable scope, distinct let variables, sort compatibility, exhaustive match cases or the logical meaning of annotations. A term satisfying it is grammatically admissible at this stage, not necessarily well sorted.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.ValidBindi: This condition applies the grammatical term restrictions to the defining term in each let binding. It imposes no nonemptiness condition on the whole list and does not require the variable names to be distinct. Nonemptiness is handled by the enclosing let-expression rule. The standard's parallel substitution semantics and distinct-name requirement are not established here.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.ValidCases: For each match case, the formal condition requires the pattern and its body to satisfy their grammatical restrictions in the selected version. It does not require the list of cases to be nonempty; that is handled by the enclosing match-expression rule. It also does not establish exhaustive matching, distinct variables, compatible sorts or the semantics of choosing a case.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.tokens: The formal definition writes the tokens of every represented term, including applications, let expressions, abstractions, quantifiers, matches and annotations. Lists may be empty in the representation, so writing tokens alone does not establish the grammar's nonemptiness conditions. The separate grammatical condition supplies those restrictions. Neither operation assigns logical meaning to the resulting term.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.SourceFile: Version 2.0 requires every byte in a source file to be below 128. For versions 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7, this particular condition imposes no restriction. It neither decodes Unicode nor establishes that an input is a valid encoding. Lexical and grammatical conditions are defined separately, and tokenisation does not automatically include this source-file condition.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Token.content: The formal definition removes the delimiters of strings and quoted symbols, decodes the appropriate string escapes, removes the colon of a keyword, and removes the #x or #b prefix of hexadecimal or binary literals. Other token text is preserved. These are conventions for what the parser receives; the declaration does not assign the logical meaning of a literal or establish symbol equality.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization: Tokenisation starts at byte offset zero and applies the version-dependent lexical rules across the entire input. Spaces and comments are omitted from the token list. The formalization also requires delimiters after non-parenthesis tokens and accepts a final comment without a newline. These choices make the relation more specific than the paper's statement that whitespace separates tokens.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization.From: The input is split into recognised tokens separated by whitespace and comments, beginning at a supplied byte offset. Each token's position includes the preceding whitespace. Non-parenthesis tokens obey the formalization's additional delimiter rule, and a final comment may end without a newline. This relation describes tokenisation; it does not enforce Unicode encoding validity or the separate source-file restriction for version 2.0.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.addedCommandNames: The formal definition lists commands when they first become available and later combines those lists across versions. It includes define-funs-rec from version 2.5 onward, and declare-sort-parameter and define-const in version 2.7. Appendix B's reserved-command list omits define-funs-rec, although the command appears in the command grammar and the main text says every command name is reserved.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.comment: A comment begins with a semicolon and contains no line feed or carriage return before its terminating line-breaking character. The terminating character is part of the matched sequence. Whether the semicolon lies outside a string or quoted symbol is determined when the surrounding input is tokenised. A separate rule admits a final comment that reaches the end of input without a line break.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.decimal: A decimal consists of a numeral, a decimal point, zero or more zeroes, and a final numeral. Consequently there is at least one digit on each side of the point, and leading zeroes are allowed only in the fractional part. The definition recognises spelling; it does not interpret the token as a rational number, floating-point value or any other theory-specific object.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.keyword: The formal definition accepts a colon followed by any nonempty sequence of letters, digits and the punctuation permitted in simple symbols. Thus a keyword may begin with a digit or use a reserved word after the colon. This follows the older rule and the paper's example :56, but is broader than the stated version 2.7 production requiring a simple symbol after the colon.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.numeral: A numeral is either the single digit 0 or a nonempty string of decimal digits whose first digit is not 0. This is a lexical rule: it rejects leading zeroes such as 01 and does not attach a numerical interpretation. As the paper explains for special constants, the surrounding theory supplies their meaning when they occur as terms.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.printableChar: The formal definition accepts one byte with value from 32 to 126 or from 128 to 255. This matches the bounded ranges printed in Appendix B. The main text instead speaks of Unicode characters from 128 onward. A character encoded in several bytes can pass the byte-based rules, but the formal definition does not decode or validate that encoding.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.quotedSymbol: A quoted symbol has a vertical bar at each end and may contain printable bytes or white space in between, except for vertical bars and backslashes. Empty quoted symbols are permitted. This rule recognises their spelling only. Obtaining the symbol's name removes the enclosing bars, while the syntax representation separately remembers that the spelling was quoted.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.simpleSymbol: A simple symbol is a nonempty sequence of ASCII letters, digits and the listed punctuation, with no initial digit and no spelling reserved by the selected version. Names beginning with @ or a dot are still recognised as symbols. Their restriction to solver use concerns where such names may be introduced; it is not imposed by this lexical definition.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.string: String literals have opening and closing double quotes. Between them, the formal definition permits printable bytes and the four white space characters, with each internal double quote represented twice. A backslash has no escaping role in this rule. The same spelling rule is used for versions 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7; version 2.0 has a separate rule.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.unescape: Given the interior of a string literal, the formal definition replaces each pair of adjacent double quotes by one double quote and preserves every other byte. Removing the surrounding quotes is performed separately when token contents are obtained. This operation assumes the intended use on a recognised string interior; it does not itself test whether the input was a well-formed literal.
notes.BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.Received.Of: For a reserved-word token, this condition requires membership in the reserved set of the selected version. Every other token or end-of-input item is accepted by this condition. It is therefore only the version-dependent reserved-word check, relying on the lexical stage for permitted spellings. It does not establish that the item is legal at its current grammatical position.
